chapters.title: Chapter 7: Extreme Value Theory for Tail Risk

lessons.title: The Generalized Pareto Distribution and the Peaks-Over-Threshold Method

children.text: The last lesson's theorem promised that exceedances beyond a sufficiently high threshold converge to a specific distributional family. This lesson makes that concrete: the Peaks-Over-Threshold method, POT, and the Generalized Pareto Distribution, GPD, it fits. Together they are the standard practical toolkit for Extreme Value Theory in risk management.

body.label: Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) Method
body.value: Choose a high threshold, collect every observation that exceeds it, and fit a Generalized Pareto Distribution to those exceedance amounts specifically
body.context: Everything below the threshold is discarded for this step, it played no role in shaping the extreme tail to begin with.

body.caption: The Generalized Pareto Distribution. y is the exceedance amount, the observed value minus the threshold u. Xi is the shape parameter, beta is the scale parameter.

children.text: The Two Parameters: Shape and Scale

body.caption: What the shape parameter xi means

cells: A genuinely heavy, fat tail, decaying as a power law, similar in spirit to a Student-t distribution's tail from the last lesson
The boundary case, an exponentially decaying tail, thinner than any xi > 0 case
A short, bounded tail, losses cannot exceed a finite maximum value

children.text: Worked Example: Fitting a GPD to 25 Exceedances

Out of 250 trading days, a threshold of u = 2.0% daily loss is chosen, and 25 days exceed it, exactly 10% of the sample. The amounts by which each of those 25 days exceeded 2.0% are recorded as the exceedance data.

body.caption: 25 exceedance amounts over the 2.0% threshold (percentage points), sorted smallest to largest
Method-of-moments estimators for the GPD, using the sample mean and variance of the exceedances. A simple, hand-computable alternative to full maximum likelihood estimation.

stats.label: Fitted xi (shape), beta (scale)
stats.context: A mildly positive xi confirms a genuine, if modest, fat tail

children.text: Extrapolating Beyond the Data: The Real Power of EVT

body.caption: VaR estimated from the fitted GPD, at increasingly extreme confidence levels

body.text: The worst single day actually observed in this entire 250-day sample was a loss of 4.10%, the 2.0% threshold plus the largest exceedance, 2.10%. The GPD-based 99.9% VaR estimate, 4.605%, is larger than that. This is not an error, it is the entire point of Extreme Value Theory: the fitted tail shape lets you estimate risk at a severity beyond anything actually observed in the sample, grounded in a theoretically justified extrapolation rather than a guess.

Recall from Chapter 2 that Historical Simulation with a small sample could not even distinguish a 95% VaR from a 99% VaR. Here, with 250 days, a 99.9% VaR would require, on average, only 0.25 exceedances, a quarter of one observation. Historical Simulation literally cannot define this quantile from this sample. The GPD fit can, precisely because it does not need an actual observed exceedance at that exact severity, it only needs enough extreme observations to estimate the shape of the tail, then extrapolates using that shape.

children.text: Choosing the Threshold: A Genuine Trade-off

Threshold choice is not free of judgment. Set it too low, and you include observations that are not extreme enough for the underlying convergence theorem to have taken hold, biasing the fitted shape. Set it too high, and too few exceedances remain to estimate xi and beta reliably, and the estimates become noisy and unstable. A common starting point in practice is the top 5% to 15% of the data, refined using diagnostic tools like a mean excess plot, which checks whether the average exceedance size behaves linearly above the chosen threshold, the signature the GPD theory predicts.

body.title: Verify the Method-of-Moments Shape Estimate
body.prompt: A different sample of exceedances has a sample mean of 0.60 and a sample variance of 0.30. Using the method-of-moments formula, xi = 0.5 x [(mean squared / variance) minus 1], what is the estimated xi?
body.explanation: mean squared = 0.36, divided by variance 0.30 gives 1.2. Subtracting 1 gives 0.2, and half of that is 0.1: xi = 0.5 x (1.2 - 1) = 0.5 x 0.2 = 0.1. This xi is larger than the worked example's 0.0355, meaning this second sample implies a fatter, heavier tail than the one fitted earlier in this lesson.

body.title: Choosing a Threshold
body.scenario: An analyst is deciding between two thresholds for a five-year daily return dataset, roughly 1,250 observations: a threshold that captures the top 20% of days as exceedances, roughly 250 observations, versus a threshold that captures only the top 1%, roughly 12 observations.
body.prompt: What is the risk of each choice, and how would you reason about which is more appropriate?
body.modelAnswer: The top 20% threshold risks including days that are not genuinely extreme, ordinary bad days rather than true tail events, which can bias the GPD fit since the convergence theorem behind GPD is only guaranteed to hold above a sufficiently high threshold. The top 1% threshold, with only about 12 observations, risks the opposite problem, too few data points to estimate xi and beta with any real precision, producing unstable, high-variance parameter estimates. A reasonable middle ground, often in the 5% to 15% range, balances having enough exceedances for stable estimation against staying high enough that the theoretical justification for using GPD actually applies, and this choice should ideally be checked with a diagnostic tool like a mean excess plot rather than picked arbitrarily.

body.text: A fitted GPD can tell you about a loss worse than anything in your data, because it models the shape of the tail rather than memorizing specific observed points. That is a fundamentally different, and fundamentally more honest, kind of extrapolation than picking the worst historical day and calling it done.

points: The Peaks-Over-Threshold method fits a Generalized Pareto Distribution specifically to exceedances beyond a chosen high threshold, discarding the rest of the data for this step.

The GPD's shape parameter xi determines tail thickness, xi greater than 0 signals a genuine fat tail, xi equal to 0 is the exponential boundary case, and xi less than 0 implies a bounded maximum loss.
In the worked example, the fitted GPD's 99.9% VaR estimate, 4.605%, exceeded the worst day actually observed in the 250-day sample, 4.10%, genuine extrapolation grounded in the fitted tail shape.
This directly resolves a limitation from Chapter 2: Historical Simulation cannot define a quantile that would require a fraction of an observed exceedance, but a properly fitted GPD can.

Threshold selection is a real trade-off between bias from too low a threshold and estimation noise from too high a threshold, commonly addressed by starting in the top 5% to 15% of the data and checking with diagnostic tools.
